title: What to do when a parent dies in the UK
dek: Check the correct registration route, arrange immediate care, and separate Tell Us Once from the banks and insurers you still need to contact.
metaDescription: Check the correct registration route, arrange immediate care, and separate Tell Us Once from the banks and insurers you still need to contact.

paragraphs: When a parent dies in the UK, first follow the care team's or emergency service's instructions, check anyone who relies on them, and identify the registration route for the nation where the death occurred. England and Wales use the medical-examiner process before registration; Scotland and Northern Ireland have their own rules.

The first difficulty may be not knowing which call is yours to make. Keep one note with the hospital or GP contact, registrar, funeral director and the person coordinating family information. This guide helps with the first fortnight; it does not determine inheritance, replace legal advice or cover every death abroad.

body.heading: Start with people and immediate risks
items: For a hospital or care-home death, ask staff who will explain verification, certification and release arrangements. For an expected home death, use the care plan or GP contact instructions. If there is an emergency or uncertainty about whether the person has died, call 999.
Arrange support for any surviving dependent, and care for pets. Check whether someone needs food, medication access, keys or transport tonight.
Secure the property and address urgent hazards. Ask the home insurer what changes if it will be unoccupied; do not assume an ordinary household policy continues unchanged.
Find any funeral wishes or prepaid plan before buying arrangements. You can speak to a funeral director while official paperwork is pending; permission for burial or cremation is a separate issue.
Locate the will and the solicitor's details. Keep the original intact and avoid promising that you can distribute property immediately.

body.heading: Registration: use the right national instructions
rows: Wait for medical-examiner confirmation that registration can proceed.
Register within five days of confirmation, including weekends and bank holidays; contact the registrar immediately if more time is needed.
Contact a Scottish registration office; the registrar needs the medical certificate.
Official Scottish guidance says within eight days of death where possible; ask about referrals or delays.
Follow NI Direct and the district registrar's instructions.
Register within five days unless referred to the coroner; ask the registrar if there is a delay.

body.heading: Why waiting for confirmation is not missing your task
paragraphs: In England and Wales, the [GOV.UK registration guidance](https://www.gov.uk/after-a-death/register-the-death) says to wait for the medical examiner's office to confirm that you can register. Do not count five days from the death and assume you have failed while certification is pending. Write down when confirmation arrives and contact the register office if the timing cannot be met.

Use [Scottish registration guidance](https://www.mygov.scot/register-death) and [NI Direct](https://www.nidirect.gov.uk/articles/registering-death-district-registrar) for those nations rather than extending the England/Wales process across the UK. A coroner or procurator fiscal referral changes the practical sequence; ask the office handling the case which document is available and what can proceed.

body.heading: Invented example: a hospital death in Leeds
paragraphs: A parent dies on Sunday. On Monday the daughter asks the hospital for the medical-examiner office contact, checks the house and talks to a funeral director about provisional arrangements. She does not invent a Wednesday registration deadline. When the examiner's office confirms registration can proceed, she records the date and contacts the registrar within the applicable window.

Meanwhile, her brother asks banks and pension providers which evidence they need. He records the answers without moving money or cancelling essential household cover. Splitting information gathering from estate transactions lets relatives help without implying they all have authority.

body.heading: Tell Us Once does not tell everyone
paragraphs: The registrar can provide the reference for [Tell Us Once](https://www.gov.uk/after-a-death/organisations-you-need-to-contact-and-tell-us-once). It is available for people who were living in England, Scotland or Wales, not Northern Ireland. Use the reference within 28 days. Check the service's current coverage, including participating pension schemes, rather than assuming every public or workplace pension is included.

Separately notify banks, building societies, private pension providers, insurers, an employer and the landlord or mortgage provider as applicable. Ask what happens to joint accounts and essential direct debits before assuming all payments should stop. Anyone receiving their own benefits linked to the deceased person should contact their paying office separately. Keep the service confirmation and remaining private contacts in the same record.

body.heading: Two calls that reduce repeat work

items.line: The death occurred in your area. Which certification must arrive before we can register, who is eligible to register, and what date should we work to if there is a delay?
I need to report a death and understand your bereavement process. What evidence do you need, which payments or survivor benefits need checking, and will you confirm the next steps in writing?

body.heading: Documents, expenses and legal boundaries
paragraphs: Before buying multiple certified copies, list who needs one and ask whether copies are returned or digital evidence is accepted. Save funeral estimates and signed contracts. The person signing may be taking on a payment obligation; do not rely on an assumed immediate release of estate funds.

Probate, confirmation in Scotland, and estate administration are not interchangeable with simply finding your name in a will. What evidence an institution requires depends on the assets and jurisdiction. Read [the UK executor guide](/guides/named-executor-what-you-agreed-to-uk) before accepting transactions as routine. Do not divide belongings or send inheritances while debts, ownership or entitlement remain unresolved.

Seek a solicitor promptly for disputed wills, suspected abuse, foreign assets, an insolvent estate, a continuing business or pressure to distribute money. Check legal and tax deadlines early; taking longer over the house does not make every estate deadline optional.

items.q: Does the five-day registration deadline run from death?
items.a: For England and Wales, current GOV.UK guidance says to register within five days of medical-examiner confirmation that you can register. Scotland and Northern Ireland have different processes. Record which national route applies and ask the relevant registrar about a referral, missing certification or a deadline you cannot meet.

items.q: Can I contact a funeral director before registration?
items.a: Yes, you can discuss arrangements while the required paperwork is pending. Do not confuse that conversation with authorization for a burial or cremation to take place. Ask the funeral director and registrar which documents are needed and whether any proposed date must remain provisional.

items.q: Does Tell Us Once close my parent's bank accounts?
items.a: No. You still need to contact banks and other private organizations through their bereavement routes. Tell Us Once covers relevant government bodies and participating schemes, not every financial provider. Keep a separate list of private contacts and check the effect on joint accounts and household payments before requesting changes.
